Tuning a sourdough starter for cold kitchens

Posted on January 9, 2026 by Lena

My kitchen rarely climbs above seventeen degrees between November and March, and for years my starter sulked through the whole winter. It rose slowly, smelled of nail varnish, and gave me dense loaves no matter how long I proofed them.

The fix turned out to be a combination of three small changes, none of which needs special equipment. I will go through them in the order I tried them, because each one helped a little on its own.

1. Feed with warmer water

Using water at around thirty degrees gives the culture a head start after each feeding. It cools down quickly, but those first hours seem to matter most, and the smell became noticeably milder within a week.

2. Change the ratio

I moved from equal parts to one part starter, three parts flour and three parts water. A larger feeding dilutes the acid, and in a cold room the yeast needs all the help it can get against the bacteria.

starter: 20 g
flour:   60 g
water:   60 g (30 C)

3. Find a warm corner

The top of the fridge, next to the back vent, stays a few degrees warmer than the counter. Moving the jar there cut the time to peak from twelve hours to about seven.
